clue.text: Restructure due — can't lay off senior Scottish lawyer

indicators.note: to restructure is to rebuild in a new form, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A firm is told to reorganise because the money owed means it cannot sack anyone, perhaps a senior advocate.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'can't' is ignored. The Dean of Faculty heads the Faculty of Advocates, the body of Scotland's barristers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dean of the Faculty of Advocates is the elected leader of the Scottish bar, so a senior Scottish lawyer.

clue.text: Reminiscent of detective finally addressing case

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word detective, taking just its closing letter

parts.note: the vocative is the grammatical case used when addressing someone

explanation.surface: A detective's closing speech on a case brings back memories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests a criminal investigation beside 'detective', but it is grammatical case.
explanation.definitionFit: Something evocative of a thing calls it to mind, just as a reminiscent object does.

clue.text: Snare pointless — change of heart required

indicators.note: the heart of the phrase, its middle letter, is swapped for a different one

parts.note: something pointless is of no use

explanation.surface: A trapper decides a snare is futile and needs a new attitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change of heart' usually means changing one's mind; here the central U of NO USE becomes O.
explanation.definitionFit: A noose is a running loop used to trap animals, which is a snare.

clue.text: Nothing winning about kiss, a second indiscretion

parts.note: FA is short for 'sweet Fanny Adams', British slang for nothing at all

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a team winning is up
X is the kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Someone keeps scoring nil while a second kiss proves a social blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet Fanny Adams' (sweet FA) is British slang for nothing at all; 'winning' is UP, as a team ahead is.
explanation.definitionFit: A faux pas is a social blunder, an act of tactlessness or indiscretion.

clue.text: Trump's behind troubles and torments

parts.note: the behind of anyone, Trump included, is the ass in American slang
what troubles you ails you

explanation.surface: Political comment: Donald Trump is the force behind all the problems and suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump's behind' reads as 'Trump is behind'; it is simply his backside.
explanation.definitionFit: To assail is to attack or plague someone, close in sense to tormenting them.

clue.text: Not yet attempted taking on males in need of grooming

indicators.note: taking on means admitting into itself, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: something not yet attempted is untried
M is the abbreviation for male, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: An untested firm hires men who need tidying up.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedge or beard left untrimmed has not been cut back and needs tidying.

clue.text: Covering miles — some flipping walk!

indicators.note: covering means wrapping around, so the reversed word encloses the letter
flipping means turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: some of something is part of it

explanation.surface: A hiker covering many miles exclaims at the length of the hike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British oath; it turns PART into TRAP, which then covers M.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk a long way with heavy steps, a hike.

clue.text: US writer ruins platonic arrangement

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An American author wrecks a friendship that was meant to stay chaste.
explanation.definitionFit: Upton Sinclair was the American novelist who wrote The Jungle.

clue.text: Jointly capitulated

parts.note: to give in by bending the knuckles under, the knuckles being finger joints, hence 'jointly'

explanation.surface: Allies surrendered together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jointly' seems to mean together, but it hints at the finger joints in the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: To knuckle under is an idiom for submitting or yielding, and the knuckle is a joint.

clue.text: Discontinues for a time supporting scoundrels

parts.note: someone supporting a cause is pro it
rogues are scoundrels

explanation.surface: A sitting is suspended because people are backing villains.
explanation.definitionFit: To prorogue parliament is to suspend its sessions without dissolving it, stopping it for a while.

clue.text: School temperature drops

parts.note: rain falls as drops

explanation.surface: A school's thermometer reading falls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' is a verb, as in schooling a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: To school someone is to teach or drill them, which is to train them.

clue.text: Old enough to finally smoke drugs

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word to, taking just its closing letter

parts.note: fag is British slang for a cigarette, a smoke
E is slang for ecstasy, so stands for drugs

explanation.surface: A teenager is at last allowed to smoke and take narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: FAG is everyday British slang for a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: Being of age means having reached the legal adult age, old enough to do something.

clue.text: Snap after Prince's angry words

definitions.note: plural phrase for a single tirade

parts.note: Prince Philip, the late Duke of Edinburgh
a snap is a photo, a pic

explanation.surface: A photographer catches the Duke of Edinburgh in one of his outbursts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' places PIC after PHILIP; Prince Philip was famed for gaffes and outbursts.
explanation.definitionFit: A philippic is a bitter verbal attack, after Demosthenes' speeches against Philip of Macedon.

clue.text: Impalers drinking Irish whiskey and brandy?

indicators.note: drinking means taking in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: spits impale meat for roasting

explanation.surface: Torturers with stakes knock back Irish whiskey and brandy.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks whiskey and brandy as examples of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiskey and brandy are both examples of distilled spirits.

clue.text: Rat in castle biting servant

indicators.note: biting holds something between the teeth, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a fort is a castle
a man is a manservant

explanation.surface: A rodent in a castle nips a servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rat' looks like the animal; it is the verb's noun sense, a betrayer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rat is slang for someone who betrays others to the authorities, an informant.

clue.text: Important lesson — change sides

indicators.note: right and left are the two sides, so R becomes L

parts.note: a seminar is a class or lesson

explanation.surface: A vital lesson about switching political allegiance.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L are the abbreviations for right and left.
explanation.definitionFit: A seminal work is hugely influential, so of great importance.

clue.text: Offset due — fill in form

indicators.note: to form is to shape, so these letters are reshaped into the answer

explanation.surface: Instructions for claiming a refund: amount owed, then fill in the form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form' reads as a noun, the paper; it is the verb signalling an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An effect that is nullified is cancelled out, or offset.

clue.text: End fuel crisis as required

indicators.note: a crisis throws things into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Ending the fuel shortage is a necessity.
explanation.definitionFit: Needful is an old-fashioned word for necessary.

clue.text: Current head of government turning into wino — that's awkward!

indicators.note: into means going inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: a lush is a drunkard

indicators.note: turning means turning round, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current
PM is the prime minister, the British head of government

explanation.surface: A prime minister turns into a drunk, which is embarrassing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' makes IPM into MPI, which goes inside LUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumpish means heavy and clumsy, hence awkward in movement.

clue.text: Cross about dates with duke — not thinking clearly

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the hybrid encloses the letters

parts.note: a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey
D is the abbreviation for date, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: Someone angry about appointments with a nobleman is confused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry; it is a cross-breed animal, and 'about' wraps it around the two dates.
explanation.definitionFit: Muddled describes a confused mind, one not thinking clearly.

clue.text: Report to me in Barking North

indicators.note: barking means mad, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: An instruction to send the report to someone in the north of Barking, a district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a London district, and 'barking' is also British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: To mention something is to refer to or report it briefly.

clue.text: Be a high street stationer — it's a stable job

definitions.note: names the job; the answer is the person who does it

parts.note: to be is to live
Ryman is a chain of stationery shops on British high streets

explanation.surface: Running a stationery shop on the high street is secure work.
explanation.walkthrough: Ryman is a British high-street stationery chain. 'Stable job' seems to mean secure employment; it points to livery stables, where horses are kept for hire.
explanation.definitionFit: A liveryman keeps or works at a livery stable, looking after horses for their owners.

clue.text: Largely failing to save edition of holy books

indicators.note: saving keeps something safe inside, so one piece holds the other
largely means most of it, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a vice is a failing

explanation.surface: Mostly unable to rescue a printing of the scriptures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Largely' drops the last letter of the synonym for failing, leaving VIC; 'to save' then holds the edition abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Vedic means relating to the Vedas, the oldest Hindu sacred texts.

clue.text: Spirit? Sounds like it

indicators.note: says the answer is pronounced like the word that follows

parts.note: it refers back to spirit taken as a drink, such as gin

explanation.surface: Is it a ghost? It seems to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' stands for a spirit in the drinks sense, gin, which is said like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A djinn is a spirit of Arabian mythology, a genie.

clue.text: Pulls grass up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: sward is an expanse of grass

explanation.surface: Someone yanks weeds out of the lawn.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw is to drag or pull something along.

clue.text: I help part of UK initially during recession

indicators.note: recession means going back, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: aid is help
NI are the initials of Northern Ireland, a part of the UK

explanation.surface: Someone offers to assist a region of Britain at first during an economic downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the speaker, but India is the NATO alphabet word for I.
explanation.definitionFit: In the international radio alphabet, India is the code word for the letter I.

clue.text: 'Not original' — university musical reviewed by Independent

parts.note: MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

indicators.note: reviewed suggests looking back over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical

explanation.surface: A newspaper critic dismisses a college show as derivative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reviewed' suggests a critic; it turns EVITA into ATIVE. 'by' places I beside the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Imitative work copies something else, so it is unoriginal.

clue.text: Stop, son! Dad ordered a drink

parts.note: to scotch a rumour is to stop it

indicators.note: ordered means put into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A child is told to stop as the father orders a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' looks like Dad placing an order at the bar; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotch and soda is a whisky mixed with soda water, a classic bar drink.
